title: Pilot weekly — dynamic throttle & burst recovery sync
summary: Weekly pilot sync focused on recent burst-induced 502/504s and timeout patterns. Reviewed telemetry, root cause hypothesis (cold KV cache + aggressive client retry), throttling policy tweaks, suggested circuit-breaker and warmup probes, and next steps for a short runbook and small config changes for the pilot.
topics: KV cache warmup and prefix caching
Security: audit logs and KMS question
action_items: Samir to share pod-level CPU/NET graphs for spike window by 2028-01-13
Maya to produce a suggested throttle config and backoff policy doc by 2028-01-14
Ethan to send pricing/commit options for dedicated warm pools by 2028-01-16
Jules to run a 30m synthetic burst test using the pilot token and share results by 2028-01-15
next_steps: Implement suggested throttle + retry policy on staging
Run controlled burst test during low-traffic window
Follow-up sync next Tuesday 2028-01-17 10:00am PT to review telemetry
Redwood to provide security checklist and SOC2 snapshot
transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-01-11 07:00 PT / Duration: 42 mins / Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (ClearWave Eng Manager), Samir Patel (ClearWave Platform), Jules Romero (ClearWave SRE)

[00:00] Ethan Park (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — audio okay? ... cool. We're the usual crew from Redwood, Ethan and Maya. Lena, Samir, Jules, thanks for time. We wanted to run through the burst-induced 5xxs you saw last Thursday and agree on small mitigation steps for the pilot.

[00:22] Lena Ortiz (ClearWave): Yeah thanks. We had a 11:12am spike, spiked to about 3x baseline QPS for 4 minutes and then a bunch of 502/504s and some client-side timeouts. It recovered once the traffic dropped but it annoyed the workflow. We've got some retained logs — I can share the rough timeline.

[00:42] Jules Romero (SRE): Small correction — it was actually 11:09, and we saw queue depth climb on the inference hosts, CPU stayed high on two nodes and networking looked fine. We saw the Redwood responses with 502 and then 504s, and our client retried quickly which made a second wave. So yeah, compounded.

[01:10] Maya Singh (Redwood SE): Okay, thanks for that. A common pattern we see is a cold KV cache plus aggressive client retries; that combos with batch sizing to create tail latencies and then 502s if we hit request timeouts. Do you have any sampling of model sequence lengths or token distribution during that minute?

[01:30] Samir Patel (Platform Eng): Mostly short sequences — like single-paragraph prompts. The token histogram spiked a bit but not huge. But the concurrency per user jumped because some frontend fan-out logic retried on every failed request. We'll attach the traces.

[01:50] Ethan Park: Great. To be explicit: our hypothesis is warmup + retry amplification. There are three levers — client retry/backoff, server-side throttle windowing, and prefix/KV caching. We'll recommend small changes on all three.

[02:07] Lena: Quick security Q early — when you talk about telemetry and traces, can you confirm PII is redacted and that logs are accessible via our audit stream? We need KMS details for the pilot.

[02:20] Maya: Yes, we redact user text in analytics by default in hosted mode, but for Dedicated we can enable customer-managed KMS and forward raw audit logs to your SIEM under the private deployment contract. I'll send the security checklist.

[02:40] Jules: Cool. Back to the incident. We noticed an odd pattern where some requests returned quick 200s and then later some 502s — sounds like a worker eviction or out-of-memory? Do you see anything server-side?

[02:55] Maya: From our telemetry, we saw elevated queuing at the model frontends and the runtime started dropping requests when queue length exceeded the soft window. That matched the timestamps. There weren't kernel-level OOMs, but two workers hit high memory transiently due to unexpected sequence concatenation from the client. The runtime has a soft circuit-breaker but it was set conservatively for pilot.

[03:28] Samir: The client code concatenates a few user events into a single request occasionally, we can throttle that. But the immediate thing we want is to avoid user-visible failures in production.

[03:40] Ethan: Understood. So immediate mitigations: 1) Mild server-side throttle change — slightly lower max concurrency per host and increase the prequeue timeout to favour graceful backpressure, 2) Client-side backoff tweak — increase initial backoff and random jitter, 3) Enable prefix caching for the most common prompt templates so KV cache reduces compute for repeats.

[04:05] Lena: For #3, how intrusive is prefix caching? Would it change model outputs in any way? We can't have regression.

[04:17] Maya: It shouldn't change outputs if configured correctly — we'd cache KV states for exact-match prefixes and only for deterministic transforms. We recommend you pick a small set of canonical prompts first. We can run A/B to ensure no regressions.

[04:36] Jules: How do we validate no regression? We have an eval suite but it's slow.

[04:45] Maya: We can run a focused eval with your golden prompts and do token-level diff and a small human check on sampled outputs — quick smoke tests.

[04:58] Samir: Can you walk through what throttle config you mean by 'soft window'?

[05:05] Maya: Sure — right now the pilot has a single fixed concurrency cap and then a 100ms prequeue before dropping. We'll propose a moving window that reduces accepted concurrency by 20% if tail latency exceeds X ms for Y seconds, and grows back slowly. Also implement a fast-fail path to return a 429 with Retry-After for request levels above emergency.

[05:33] Ethan: Also recommend adding a client-side awareness: if you get 429s or 5xxs, backoff with exponential jitter and do not immediately fan-out retries across multiple endpoints.

[05:46] Lena: Our frontend currently retries three times with no jitter. We can change that.

[05:50] Jules: One more note — during the spike the worker processes seemed to recycle; we suspect GC thrash. Have you seen GC-triggered latency on similar pilots?

[06:00] Maya: Yes, we have seen that on long-lived processes when prefix sizes grow unexpectedly. Our runtime now supports memory soft-limits and incremental checkpointing; we can tune GC thresholds or restart less aggressively during bursts.

[06:18] Samir: What's the rollback risk if we change throttle config during the pilot? I mean, could it make things worse for normal traffic?

[06:26] Maya: We'll start conservative and run the changes in staging for a short soak. For production, a canary rollout to a small percentage of traffic (5-10%) then increase while monitoring key metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, 5xx rate, queue depth.

[06:45] Ethan: For the pilot, we can reserve a tiny warm pool — Redwood Dedicated warm instances — or if you're on hosted we can configure dedicated burst capacity as a short-term safety valve. That reduces cold starts and reduce KV misses.

[06:58] Lena: Cost is a concern — warm pools add cost. We want to understand unit economics. Could you send an estimate for a 2-node warm pool reserved for a month so we can compare?

[07:10] Ethan: Absolutely. I'll include that in the pricing note. Also note we have an Optimize recommendation that suggests quantization or batching changes that can reduce cost and memory usage for this workload.

[07:24] Samir: On quantization — are there output quality regressions to worry about?

[07:29] Maya: For the models you're using, minimal. We advise trying 8-bit quantization for the tail model variant; the eval can detect regressions. We'll recommend a specific quant profile.

[07:43] Lena: Is there any way to give the runtime hints from the client about expected sequence length to help scheduling?

[07:50] Maya: Yes, you can pass an approximate_context_size header and a prompt_category tag. Runtime uses that to pick kernel paths and preallocate buffer sizes.

[07:58] Jules: Okay, let's talk timeline. What can be done in the next 48-72 hours vs needs more time?

[08:05] Maya: In 48 hours: Maya and Ethan can propose throttle config and client retry guidance; Redwood can enable prefix caching for a couple of canonical prompts in staging. In 72 hours: run a synthetic burst test and share telemetry.

[08:22] Ethan: We'll also prepare a short runbook for oncall — quick triage steps, what to escalate to Redwood, how to collect traces and logs.

[08:32] Lena: Perfect. Also, can Redwood provide a short script for synthetic burst test so we run it identically to your staging harness?

[08:40] Maya: Yes, we have a load generator and we'll share the script and a small config to reproduce the pattern. It uses randomized user IDs to avoid cache super-warm issues unless you want deterministic.

[08:57] Samir: On the logging side — we saw that the request ids in our logs don't always map to Redwood trace ids. Can we get a mapping or correlated ids in your audit stream?

[09:08] Maya: Yep, we can include cross-trace IDs and forward them. That will help correlate client-side retries and server-side queueing.

[09:17] Jules: One more: during the event we saw a higher rate of 502s from a shard in eu-west-1, is there any chance this was regional capacity shifting?

[09:28] Maya: It's possible. Our routing is region-aware and should have fallbacks but sometimes if one shard hits thermal throttle, it reduces capacity. We'll check hardware telemetry and routing decisions in that window.

[09:42] Ethan: Okay let's capture concrete action items — I'm going to read them and you call-backs if wrong.

[09:50] Ethan: Samir will share pod-level CPU and network graphs for spike windows by Friday (2028-01-13).

[09:58] Samir: Yep, I'll get that.

[10:00] Ethan: Maya will draft throttle and backoff config and example client changes by Saturday (2028-01-14).

[10:06] Maya: Yep.

[10:08] Ethan: Jules will run a 30 minute synthetic burst using pilot token and share results Monday (2028-01-15).

[10:15] Jules: I'll schedule it.

[10:17] Ethan: I will send dedicated/warm pool pricing and an Optimize recommendation by Monday (2028-01-16) and include KMS details and SOC2 pointer.

[10:26] Ethan: Any blockers or questions before we wrap?

[10:30] Lena: Only one — can Redwood add a short customer-managed webhook that triggers a graceful degrade mode in our client? Say if an external alarm from Redwood says 'enter degrade', our frontend can drop to safe mode.

[10:44] Maya: We have a lightweight webhook for routing signals. We can set up a control plane flag with low-latency messaging for your frontend to listen to. We'll include the interface in the runbook.

[10:55] Samir: Great. Also, if you could include a short note about how the adaptive throttle plays with our rate limits. We have an existing API gateway throttle.

[11:04] Maya: We'll document interactions. Ideally the gateway rate limits at a slightly higher level and let the runtime do finer-grained per-host throttling; we'll note recommended thresholds.

[11:15] Ethan: Alright, quick recap: throttle + backoff changes, prefix cache in staging, synthetic test, runbook, pricing for warm pool, and security checklist. Follow-up sync Tuesday 2028-01-17 10am PT. Anything else?

[11:28] Lena: No, that covers it. Thanks everyone.

[11:32] Ethan: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with docs and links in the next 24 hours.

[11:38] -- end of meeting --

Notes on transcription: some overlapping speech near 06:00 and 11:00, occasional mis-heard model names (eg 'Redwood Dedicate' -> 'Redwood Dedicated' intended), proper nouns may be garbled in places. Attendees agreed on next steps.
